Farce

FARSS -- one syllable, rhymes with 'sparse.' · noun

Hear It

What It Means

Farce is an absurd event or play; a mockery.

The safety drill became a farce when half the staff marched confidently to the wrong exits.

Worked Example

The drama club stages an old comedy in which two identical suitcases, three slamming doors, and one very confused waiter keep the audience howling: every character keeps grabbing the wrong bag at exactly the wrong moment.

That play is a farce in the theatrical sense: a comedy built on ridiculous, exaggerated situations. The word's second, sharper sense calls any real event a farce when it becomes so absurd it mocks what it was supposed to be -- a 'debate' where no one may ask questions, an 'inspection' done from the parking lot.

How Farce Sits Among Its Neighbors

Synonyms — open each to see how it differs

mockery

mockery: an absurd, insulting imitation of what something should be

sham

sham: a thing that is not what it pretends to be

absurdity

absurdity: something wildly unreasonable or ridiculous

Antonyms

triumph

triumph: a great, genuine success

solemnity

solemnity: deep seriousness and dignity

How Strong Is It? — absurdity → farce → mockery

absurdity vs. farce

absurdity vs. farce: An absurdity is any single ridiculous thing, while a farce is a whole event gone ridiculous -- absurdities are the ingredients; the farce is the finished dish.

mockery vs. farce

mockery vs. farce: Mockery is the strongest and angriest: calling the hearing a farce says it collapsed into nonsense, but calling it a mockery of justice says the collapse insulted the very thing it was supposed to honor.

Build the Word

The pieces

Put it together

Put it together: Farce comes from Latin farcire, 'to stuff' -- the same word cooks used for stuffing meat. Medieval performers 'stuffed' short comic skits between the acts of serious plays, and the stuffing stole the show: farce became the name for the absurd comedy itself.

Use the root in a new word: farcical

Use the root in a new word: farcical: The meeting turned farcical when both projectors failed and the fire alarm joined in.

Word Building

Word Choice

Farce carries two licensed senses -- pick one per sentence and hold it. As theater, it is a comedy of ridiculous situations (slamming doors, mistaken identities). As criticism, it brands a real event a mockery of its own purpose: the election was a farce, the inspection was a farce. It is stronger than 'a mess' -- a farce does not merely fail; it makes the thing it replaced look like a joke.
